name: Working with Guru Graphics
description: How design and brand work runs, from brief to handover.

groups.offer: Guru Graphics engagement or offer term
groups.help: way of working together and getting help

cards.subject: Brand Discovery
says: is the first of the four Guru Graphics engagements
typically takes 3 to 4 weeks
includes four original identity concepts
includes two rounds of revision on the selected route
cards.use: want a researched positioning and a core identity as a starting point
not: includes a 30 to 60 page set of brand guidelines
is a fixed-price package with a Book Now button

cards.subject: Identity Programme
says: typically takes 6 to 8 weeks
adds complete business stationery to everything in Brand Discovery
adds presentation and document templates and a digital asset library
hands over editable working files
cards.use: need day-to-day business assets as well as a logo
not: typically takes 8 to 12 weeks
is scoped per organisation with no typical duration

cards.subject: Brand System
says: typically takes 8 to 12 weeks
includes 30 to 60 page brand guidelines
adds brand voice, writing tone and campaign style rules
includes accessibility and contrast standards
cards.use: want one written system that keeps the brand consistent across teams
not: is the only engagement that includes logo variations

cards.subject: Rollout Programme
says: is scoped per organisation rather than given a typical duration
adds a launch kit for every owned channel
adds an estate, signage and print rollout plan
includes a post-launch review and support window
cards.use: need the new identity introduced across many channels and sites
not: typically takes 3 to 4 weeks

cards.subject: Request a proposal
says: is the call to action on each Guru Graphics engagement
leads to an engagement scoped and quoted against your own requirements
cards.use: want a quote for one of the four engagements
not: adds an engagement to a basket at a fixed price

cards.subject: Start a Conversation
says: is the closing invitation on the Guru Graphics site
asks you to say where your organisation is today and where the brand should go
helps the studio advise on the right level of identity support
cards.use: are not sure which level of identity support you need
not: is a button for buying a ready-made package

cards.subject: A complete brand identity system
says: is what Guru Graphics promises rather than just a logo
covers strategy, visual identity and brand messaging together
cards.use: want to know what Guru Graphics means by a brand
not: means a single logo file delivered on its own

cards.subject: The scope of Guru Graphics
says: is design and branding only
does not include software, development, hosting or support
cards.use: wonder whether the studio can build or host your website
not: includes web hosting and software support

cards.subject: The cumulative engagement ladder
says: means each Guru Graphics engagement includes everything in the one before
means Brand System contains the Identity Programme work
cards.use: compare what the four engagements contain
not: means the four engagements are separate options with no overlap

cards.subject: Brand Strategy
says: defines positioning, personality, audience, values and brand direction
is step 01 of the Guru Graphics process
gives the later design work a reason for every choice
cards.use: need to decide who the brand is for and what it stands for
not: delivers the final stationery and signage

cards.subject: Visual Identity
says: produces a distinctive logo, colour palette, typography and imagery
creates the visual language of the brand
is step 02 of the Guru Graphics process
cards.use: want the look of the brand designed
not: writes the rules for how teams must apply the brand

cards.subject: Brand Guidelines
says: set out how the brand should look, sound and behave across every touchpoint
keep the brand consistent across every platform and communication
are step 03 of the Guru Graphics process
cards.use: want your own staff and suppliers to apply the brand consistently
not: are produced before the positioning is agreed

cards.subject: Brand Applications
says: translate the identity into real touchpoints
range from signage and stationery to digital media and presentations
are step 04 of the Guru Graphics process
cards.use: want to see the identity working on real items
not: define the audience and values

cards.subject: Brand Launch
says: equips teams with creative assets and direction to introduce the identity
is step 05 of the Guru Graphics process
helps your people introduce the new identity with confidence
cards.use: are ready to introduce the new brand to your people and public
not: is the stage where the positioning is first defined

cards.subject: Brand messaging
says: shapes tone of voice, key messages and story
is one of the three pillars alongside strategy and visual identity
cards.use: need to decide how the brand speaks rather than how it looks
not: keeps colour and typography consistent

cards.subject: The background section of a brief
says: explains who the organisation is and what it does
gives the designer the context for the project
cards.use: want the designer to understand your organisation before they sketch
not: lists the file formats to be delivered
like: The objectives section of a brief

cards.subject: The objectives section of a brief
says: states what the project must achieve
lets designs be judged against a goal rather than taste
cards.use: want to say what a successful result looks like
not: describes the history of the company
like: The success measures section of a brief

cards.subject: The audience section of a brief
says: describes who the work is for
helps the designer choose tone, imagery and channels
cards.use: need the designer to know the people who will see the brand
not: lists who has authority to sign off
like: The stakeholders section of a brief

cards.subject: The scope and deliverables section of a brief
says: lists what is to be produced
prevents a mismatch between what you expect and what is quoted
cards.use: want to agree exactly which items will be delivered
not: names the project budget
like: The budget section of a brief

cards.subject: The timeline section of a brief
says: sets out key dates and fixed deadlines
tells the designer about launches or events the work must meet
cards.use: have a launch date the work must meet
not: describes the target audience
like: The scope and deliverables section of a brief

cards.subject: The budget section of a brief
says: tells the designer the spending range for the work
lets the studio recommend an engagement that fits
cards.use: want proposals that match what you can spend
not: is optional for a project with fixed scope
like: The timeline section of a brief

cards.subject: The stakeholders section of a brief
says: names who must be consulted and who decides
avoids surprise objections late in a project
cards.use: have several departments that will have a view
not: describes who buys your product
like: The audience section of a brief

cards.subject: The mandatories section of a brief
says: lists elements that cannot change, such as a legal name or a required line
stops the designer exploring routes that cannot be used
cards.use: have items that must appear or must stay as they are
not: lists the colours the designer would like to use

cards.subject: The references section of a brief
says: shows examples of work you like or dislike, with reasons
gives a shared visual vocabulary
cards.use: find it easier to show than to describe a style
not: replaces the need for an objectives section

cards.subject: The success measures section of a brief
says: states how you will judge whether the work has done its job
turns approval into a check against evidence
cards.use: want to judge the result later against agreed criteria
not: lists the project deadlines
like: The objectives section of a brief

cards.subject: A concept route
says: is a distinct design direction presented for you to react to
differs from other routes in idea, not just in colour
is chosen from a set of routes presented by the studio
cards.use: are shown several different directions for the same brand
not: is a finished set of artwork ready for print

cards.subject: A mood board
says: collects images, colours and textures to convey a feeling
is used to agree a direction before detailed design
cards.use: want to agree the look and feel before logos are drawn
not: is the final set of master artwork files

cards.subject: The selected route
says: is the concept you choose to develop further
receives the rounds of revision in Brand Discovery
cards.use: have picked one of the presented concepts to continue with
not: is the first draft of the brief

cards.subject: A design rationale
says: explains why a design choice was made in terms of the brief
helps you judge a concept against objectives rather than taste
cards.use: want to understand the reasoning behind a concept
not: lists the file formats supplied

cards.subject: A mock-up
says: shows a design applied to a realistic item such as a sign or a document
helps you picture a logo in use
cards.use: want to see how a logo looks on a real application
not: is an editable working file for the printer

cards.subject: A positioning statement
says: says what the brand offers, to whom and why it is different
guides the choice of tone and design
cards.use: need a single statement of where the brand sits among its peers
not: is a short memorable line used in advertising

cards.subject: A brand personality
says: describes the brand as a set of human traits
guides the tone of voice and the look together
cards.use: want to describe the brand as a person would be described
not: is a rule for how large the logo must be

cards.subject: A strapline
says: is a short memorable line that sits with the logo or in campaigns
expresses the brand idea in a few words
cards.use: want a short line to accompany the name
not: states the audience and competitors in a paragraph

cards.subject: Brand values
says: are the beliefs the brand wants to be known for
are defined during brand strategy
cards.use: want to say what the organisation stands for
not: are the colours of the palette

cards.subject: Consolidated feedback
says: combines the views of all your reviewers into one response
spares the designer from contradictory instructions
cards.use: have several people in your organisation reviewing the same concepts
not: means sending each reviewer's comments separately as they arrive

cards.subject: Feedback against the brief
says: measures a design against the agreed objectives and audience
keeps a discussion about design objective
cards.use: want to judge a concept fairly
not: is based on what your favourite colour is

cards.subject: A subjective reaction
says: says what you like or dislike without giving a reason
gives the designer little to act on
cards.use: say I just do not like it without a reason
not: is the most helpful form of feedback

cards.subject: Specific feedback
says: says what you want changed and why
references the part of the design rather than the whole
cards.use: want a revision to land on the first attempt
not: is a single word such as nicer

cards.subject: A round of revision
says: is one cycle of your feedback followed by the designer's amended work
is limited in number within an engagement
cards.use: want to know how many times changes can be requested
not: is a fresh set of unrelated concepts

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is the gradual addition of requests beyond what was agreed
can extend timelines and costs
cards.use: keep adding new requests after the scope was agreed
not: happens only when the designer misses a deadline

cards.subject: Design by committee
says: blends many opinions until the design loses its clear idea
is avoided by naming one decision-maker
cards.use: find every reviewer wants their own change in the logo
not: is a recommended way to sharpen a concept

cards.subject: A named decision-maker
says: is one person with authority to approve for your organisation
settles disagreements between reviewers
cards.use: want approvals not to stall between departments
not: is chosen by the designer rather than by the client

cards.subject: A feedback deadline
says: is the agreed date by which comments are due
keeps the project timeline on track
cards.use: want your launch date to hold
not: is the date a project is first invoiced

cards.subject: Testing with the audience
says: checks a concept with the people it is meant for
produces evidence in place of internal opinion
cards.use: find internal reviewers disagree and have the time to ask real users
not: replaces the need for any brief

cards.subject: An AI file
says: is the editable master artwork format of Adobe Illustrator
keeps shapes as vectors that scale without loss
cards.use: are a designer or printer needing to edit a logo
not: is the right file to paste into a word processor

cards.subject: A PDF file
says: can hold vector artwork and fonts in one document
is common for guidelines and print-ready proofs
cards.use: need a document everyone can open and print
not: is a bitmap format for web photographs

cards.subject: An SVG file
says: is a vector format used on websites
scales to any size without becoming blurry
cards.use: need a logo that is sharp on any screen size
not: is the standard format for photographs

cards.subject: A JPG file
says: is a compressed bitmap format suited to photographs
does not support transparency
cards.use: need a small file of a photograph
not: keeps a logo sharp when enlarged
supports transparent backgrounds

cards.subject: A PNG file
says: is a bitmap format that supports transparent backgrounds
is a good choice for a logo placed over a coloured background on screen
cards.use: need a logo with a clear background for a slide or web page
not: scales without limit like a vector file

cards.subject: An EPS file
says: is an older vector format often requested by printers
can be opened by many design and print programs
cards.use: are asked by a printer for a vector logo
not: is the standard format for web photographs

cards.subject: Editable working files
says: let another designer change the artwork later
are handed over with the Identity Programme
cards.use: want your own team or a new designer to adapt the artwork later
not: are flattened pictures that cannot be changed

cards.subject: Master artwork
says: is the definitive original from which other files are made
is supplied by Guru Graphics in AI, PDF, SVG, JPG and PNG
cards.use: want the source version of your logo
not: is a low-resolution preview

cards.subject: Font files
says: are required to display typography as designed
are subject to a licence that limits who may use them
cards.use: need to use the brand typeface in your own documents
not: can be freely copied to any supplier

cards.subject: RGB
says: is the colour model used for screens
builds colours from red, green and blue light
cards.use: are preparing artwork for a website or presentation
not: is the standard model for ink on paper

cards.subject: CMYK
says: is the colour model used in standard print
builds colours from cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink
cards.use: are preparing artwork for a leaflet or stationery
not: is the colour model for light emitted from screens

cards.subject: Pantone
says: is a standard system for matching a named colour exactly
helps a brand colour look the same across suppliers
cards.use: need a brand colour to match across printers
not: describes the screen resolution of a file

cards.subject: A HEX code
says: is a six-character value for a colour on screens
starts with a hash sign
cards.use: need to specify a brand colour in a web or digital setting
not: is used by printers to specify ink

cards.subject: A vector graphic
says: is built from mathematical paths
can be enlarged to any size without losing sharpness
cards.use: need a logo for both a business card and a billboard
not: is made of a fixed grid of pixels

cards.subject: A raster image
says: is made of a fixed grid of pixels
becomes blurry when enlarged beyond its size
cards.use: are working with a photograph
not: scales to any size without loss

cards.subject: Image resolution
says: is the amount of detail in a raster image
is measured in pixels, or dots per inch for print
cards.use: find a picture looks pixelated in print
not: is the same for vector files at any size

cards.subject: Bleed
says: is artwork extending past the trim edge of a print job
prevents white slivers when a page is cut
cards.use: have a design with colour running to the edge of the page
not: is a margin of empty space inside the page

cards.subject: Crop marks
says: show where a printed sheet is to be trimmed
sit outside the trimmed page area
cards.use: are sending artwork to a printer who will cut it down
not: add a coloured border to the final piece

cards.subject: A colour profile
says: tells devices how to interpret colour values
helps a colour look consistent between screen and print
cards.use: find the colour on your screen differs from the printed result
not: decides the file size of a logo

cards.subject: Transparency
says: lets a logo sit over any background without a box around it
is supported by PNG and SVG but not JPG
cards.use: want to place a logo on a coloured slide
not: is supported by every image format

cards.subject: A logo
says: is the central mark that identifies an organisation
is only one part of a full brand identity
cards.use: want the mark that identifies the organisation
not: is the same thing as the whole brand identity

cards.subject: Logo variations
says: are alternate versions of the logo for different layouts and backgrounds
typically include versions for light and dark backgrounds
cards.use: need a logo that fits a narrow banner or a dark background
not: are different logos for different companies

cards.subject: A colour palette
says: is the set of colours the brand uses
usually has primary colours and supporting colours
cards.use: want to know which colours the brand uses
not: is the set of typefaces used by the brand

cards.subject: A typography system
says: sets out the typefaces and how they are used for headings and body text
gives consistent hierarchy to written materials
cards.use: need to know which fonts to use in a report
not: is the list of colours for the brand

cards.subject: Imagery style
says: defines the look of photographs and illustration used by the brand
keeps pictures on-brand even when many people choose them
cards.use: are choosing photographs for a campaign
not: defines the size of the logo

cards.subject: A visual language
says: is the combined system of logo, colour, type, imagery and shapes
makes materials recognisable as one brand without the name
cards.use: want everything to feel like one brand even without a logo
not: is the legal name of the company

cards.subject: Brand voice
says: is the way the brand sounds in writing
is set out in the Brand System engagement as writing tone
cards.use: need to write a web page in the brand's style
not: is the order in which logo versions are used

cards.subject: A brand story
says: is the narrative of where the brand comes from and what it stands for
gives consistent material for introductions and presentations
cards.use: are asked to explain the organisation in a short narrative
not: is a list of file formats

cards.subject: A favicon
says: is the small icon shown in a browser tab
is part of the Identity Programme as favicon and channel icons
cards.use: want your site to show your icon in a browser tab
not: is a large poster-sized logo

cards.subject: A digital asset library
says: is a shared store of approved brand files
lets people find the right logo or template without asking for it
cards.use: want staff to get approved files from one place
not: is a printed binder of logo samples

cards.subject: Clear space
says: is the empty area kept around a logo
stops other text or images crowding the mark
cards.use: are placing a logo near a headline or photograph
not: is the smallest size a logo may appear

cards.subject: Minimum size
says: is the smallest dimension at which a logo stays legible
sets a floor below which the logo should not be reproduced
cards.use: want to put the logo on a small item such as a pen
not: is the empty area around the logo

cards.subject: Logo misuse
says: includes stretching, recolouring or adding effects to a logo
weakens recognition of the brand
cards.use: feel tempted to squash the logo into a gap
not: is allowed whenever the layout needs it

cards.subject: Using the approved variant
says: means choosing the logo version made for the background
avoids low contrast and unreadable marks
cards.use: are putting the logo on a dark photograph
not: means recolouring the main logo by hand

cards.subject: Choosing the right file for the job
says: matches the format to where the artwork will be used
uses vector files for print and signage
cards.use: need to decide which version of a logo to send a printer
not: means always sending the smallest file

cards.subject: Using templates as supplied
says: keeps layouts and styles consistent across teams
reduces the risk of off-brand documents
cards.use: are creating a presentation with the brand's template
not: means rebuilding the layout from scratch each time

cards.subject: Using the brand fonts
says: keeps typography consistent in documents
requires licensed font files on your computer
cards.use: are writing documents in the brand typeface
not: can be skipped when a similar font looks close enough

cards.subject: Co-branding
says: places two organisations' marks together
needs agreed rules for spacing and prominence
cards.use: are producing an item with a partner's logo beside yours
not: means merging two logos into a new one automatically

cards.subject: Asking before altering
says: means checking with the brand owner before changing approved artwork
protects consistency
cards.use: feel a change to a logo would solve a local layout problem
not: is unnecessary for small tweaks

cards.subject: Updating to the current guidelines
says: means replacing old copies of brand files when the guidelines change
stops outdated logos staying in use
cards.use: find an older logo still on a supplier's website
not: means keeping every old version in circulation

cards.subject: Brand Guidelines as a reference
says: are the first place to check before using the brand
show how the brand should look, sound and behave
cards.use: are unsure whether you can use a logo a certain way
not: are meant to be read once and filed

cards.subject: A sign-off
says: is your formal approval of a stage of work
lets the project move to the next step
cards.use: are happy with a stage and want the studio to proceed
not: is a request for further changes

cards.subject: A change request
says: is a request to alter agreed work or scope
may affect time and cost
cards.use: want something added after approval
not: is a final approval of a stage

cards.subject: A proof
says: is a preview of print work for checking before production
catches errors before they are printed
cards.use: are asked to check text and colours before a print run
not: is the original master file of the logo

cards.subject: Written approval
says: records your agreement in an email or document
can be referred back to if a question arises
cards.use: agree a change over the phone
not: is unnecessary once you have spoken in a meeting

cards.subject: A licence
says: grants permission to use something under set terms
can limit where, how long or for what purpose
cards.use: use an image, font or asset owned by someone else
not: transfers full ownership to the user

cards.subject: A font licence
says: sets out how many people and what uses a typeface may have
may need extending for more staff or web use
cards.use: want to install the brand font on more computers
not: comes automatically with any copy of a font file

cards.subject: A stock image licence
says: sets the permitted uses of a purchased photograph
may restrict use as part of a logo
cards.use: want to use a stock photograph in a campaign
not: lets you use the image anywhere forever

cards.subject: Intellectual property
says: covers rights in a creative work such as a logo
is dealt with in the agreement between client and studio
cards.use: want to know who owns the finished logo
not: always passes to the client the moment work starts

cards.subject: A trade mark
says: is a registered right in a name or logo to identify a business
needs an application to register
cards.use: want legal protection for a new name or logo
not: is created simply by designing a logo

cards.subject: A confidentiality agreement
says: keeps shared information private between the parties
covers unreleased brand work
cards.use: are sharing plans that must not leak before launch
not: is the approval of a design concept

cards.subject: Business stationery
says: is the set of everyday printed items such as letterheads and cards
is included in the Identity Programme
cards.use: need printed and digital stationery with the new identity
not: is the 30 to 60 page guidelines document

cards.subject: Presentation and document templates
says: let your staff produce on-brand slides and documents
are included from the Identity Programme
cards.use: need staff to produce on-brand slides without a designer
not: are the logo master files only

cards.subject: A launch kit
says: gives each owned channel ready assets for introducing the new identity
is part of the Rollout Programme
cards.use: are about to introduce the new identity on your channels
not: is part of Brand Discovery

cards.subject: A staff toolkit
says: helps internal teams introduce and use the identity
is part of the Rollout Programme
cards.use: want your own people ready for the launch
not: is a print-ready logo file

cards.subject: An estate, signage and print rollout plan
says: plans how the identity reaches buildings, signs and printed material
is part of the Rollout Programme
cards.use: have many sites and signs to change
not: is included in Brand Discovery

cards.subject: Governance and asset management setup
says: establishes who controls changes and where approved files live
is part of the Rollout Programme
cards.use: want to keep the brand under control after launch
not: is a printed copy of the logo

cards.subject: Templates for each publishing team
says: give teams that publish content their own on-brand formats
are part of the Rollout Programme
cards.use: have several teams that publish materials independently
not: are included in Brand Discovery

cards.subject: A post-launch review
says: checks how the identity has landed after launch
comes with a support window in the Rollout Programme
cards.use: want to learn what has worked after the new identity is live
not: is carried out before the concepts are presented

cards.subject: Handover materials
says: are the files and notes passed to the client at the end
are part of Rollout and Launch
cards.use: are at the end of the project and need everything in one place
not: are the first sketches

cards.subject: The Brand Identity item of what you get
says: covers logo systems, brand colours, typography and visual language
is one of the four things Guru Graphics says you get
cards.use: want to know what is in the Brand Identity part of what you get
not: covers stationery, templates and daily-use applications

cards.subject: Business Assets
says: are the stationery, templates, presentation assets and digital icons in daily use
are one of the four things Guru Graphics says you get
cards.use: want to know the daily-use items in your package
not: are the rules for how the brand sounds

cards.subject: A single point of contact
says: is one person on your side who talks to the studio
keeps instructions consistent
cards.use: want questions and feedback to go through one route
not: is a ticketing system for support tickets

cards.subject: A direct line to the team
says: is possible because Guru Graphics is a small studio
means clients deal with the people doing the work
cards.use: wonder who you will speak to at Guru Graphics
not: means all questions go through a call centre

cards.subject: A written call summary
says: records what was agreed in a meeting
lets everyone confirm decisions
cards.use: left a call with several decisions
not: replaces the need to agree anything in writing

cards.subject: A project timeline
says: shows the stages and dates of the project
depends on feedback arriving when agreed
cards.use: want to know when you will see the next stage
not: is a guarantee of delivery dates regardless of feedback

cards.subject: Asking early
says: means raising questions as soon as they arise
gets a doubt answered before further work builds on it
cards.use: are unsure about a part of the brief
not: means waiting until the final stage to raise doubts

cards.subject: Referring to a version
says: means naming the file, page and version when you comment
avoids confusion between drafts
cards.use: have several drafts of one concept in circulation
not: means describing the colour only

cards.subject: Sharing materials in one place
says: keeps files in a single shared location
avoids lost attachments and old versions
cards.use: have logos and documents spread across several emails
not: means sending files by separate messages to each person

cards.subject: Sharing existing brand material
says: means giving the studio your current logo, documents and guidelines
helps the studio see what already exists
cards.use: have an existing brand being refreshed
not: is unnecessary because the studio starts blank

cards.subject: Explaining your sector
says: helps the studio design for the way your organisation works
matters for medium-sized enterprises and public sector bodies
cards.use: work in a regulated or public sector setting
not: is unnecessary because design is the same everywhere

cards.subject: Procurement paperwork
says: is the set of forms and checks a buyer may need from suppliers
may be requested from the studio early
cards.use: must go through your organisation's buying process
not: is only needed after the project ends

cards.subject: Contrast standards
says: define how clearly text stands out from its background
are part of the Brand System engagement
cards.use: want text on brand colours to be easy to read
not: decide the order of the stationery

cards.subject: WCAG
says: are the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
set a widely used contrast ratio for text on web pages
cards.use: want to know the standard behind accessible web design
not: is a file format for logos

cards.subject: Alt text
says: is a text description of an image for people who cannot see it
is read aloud by screen readers
cards.use: are publishing an image on a web page
not: is the font used in the logo

cards.subject: Not relying on colour alone
says: means information is also given by text or shape
helps people with colour vision deficiency
cards.use: use red and green to mark status in a chart
not: means using only black and white

cards.subject: Plain language
says: uses short, familiar words
helps more people understand a message
cards.use: are writing a public-facing page
not: means making copy sound informal and inexact

cards.subject: Consent on a form
says: means telling people what their data is used for and linking the policy
applies to the Guru Graphics enquiry form and newsletter
cards.use: are collecting email addresses on a website
not: is satisfied by a pre-ticked box

cards.subject: Unsubscribing
says: means every edition of a newsletter lets you stop receiving it
is promised by the Guru Graphics newsletter
cards.use: want to leave a mailing list
not: is possible only once a year

cards.subject: Permission to show a logo
says: means getting written agreement before displaying another organisation's mark
applies to a clients wall
cards.use: want to show a partner's logo on your website
not: is not needed if the logo was found online

cards.subject: Unedited testimonials
says: are published exactly as the client wrote them
avoid misleading readers
cards.use: are publishing a customer quote
not: can be tidied to sound better

cards.subject: Company details on a website
says: include the registered name, number, place of registration and registered office for UK limited companies
are shown in the Guru Graphics footer
cards.use: are launching a website for a UK limited company
not: are needed only for charities

cards.subject: A reputation focus for public sector
says: frames branding around trust, recognition and standing apart
avoids the word growth for public sector audiences
cards.use: are writing for a public sector buyer
not: leads with sales growth targets

qa.q: What does Guru Graphics do?
qa.right: Brand identity design and branding
qa.why: The studio does design and branding only.

qa.q: How many steps are in the Guru Graphics brand process?
qa.right: Five
qa.why: The five steps run from Brand Strategy to Brand Launch.

qa.q: Which step of the brand process comes first?
qa.right: Brand Strategy
qa.why: Strategy defines positioning and direction before design.

qa.q: What is a design brief?
qa.right: A written description of the project goals, audience, scope and constraints
wrong: A finished logo ready for print
A list of fonts the studio owns
qa.why: The brief is the starting point that everyone designs against.

qa.q: Which file type is best for a photograph on a web page?
qa.right: JPG
qa.why: JPG compresses photographs to small sizes.

qa.q: Which colour model is used for screens?
qa.right: RGB
qa.why: Screens emit light built from red, green and blue.

qa.q: What is a logo?
qa.right: The central mark identifying an organisation, one part of a brand identity
wrong: The complete brand identity by itself
A written set of company policies
qa.why: A brand identity also includes colour, type and more.

qa.q: Who do clients deal with at Guru Graphics?
qa.right: The people doing the work, because it is a small studio
wrong: A separate sales team that passes on messages
qa.why: The studio stays close to clients.

qa.q: What does the Request a proposal button on an engagement lead to?
qa.right: A proposal scoped and quoted for your requirements
wrong: An immediate purchase at a fixed price
A free copy of the guidelines
qa.why: Engagements are scoped and quoted, not sold as packages.

qa.q: Which engagement typically takes 3 to 4 weeks?
qa.right: Brand Discovery
qa.why: Brand Discovery is the shortest, typically 3 to 4 weeks.

qa.q: How many original identity concepts does Brand Discovery include?
qa.right: Four
qa.why: Four concepts are presented, then two revision rounds on the chosen route.

qa.q: How many rounds of revision on the selected route does Brand Discovery include?
qa.right: Two
qa.why: Brand Discovery includes two rounds of revision.

qa.q: Which engagement typically includes 30 to 60 page brand guidelines?
qa.right: Brand System
qa.why: The guidelines come with the Brand System.

qa.q: Which engagement is scoped per organisation rather than given a typical duration?
qa.right: Rollout Programme
qa.why: Rollout is scoped for each organisation.

qa.q: What does it mean that each engagement includes everything in the one before?
qa.right: The Brand System includes the Identity Programme and Brand Discovery work
wrong: The engagements are alternatives with no overlap
You pay separately for each earlier stage
qa.why: The engagements build upwards.

qa.q: Which file keeps a logo sharp at any size?
qa.right: A vector file such as SVG or AI
wrong: A small PNG of a thumbnail
qa.why: Vectors are made from paths, not pixels.

qa.q: Why is feedback against the brief more useful than a personal reaction?
qa.right: It lets the designer act on measurable goals
wrong: It removes the need for revisions
qa.why: Objective feedback gives the designer something to change.

qa.q: Which statement about durations in the engagements is correct?
qa.right: They are typical rather than promised
qa.why: Typical durations depend on scope and feedback.

qa.q: Why does a logo have light and dark variations?
qa.right: So it stays legible on different backgrounds
qa.why: The right variant avoids poor contrast.

qa.q: What does CMYK describe?
qa.right: The inks used in standard print
qa.why: Cyan, magenta, yellow and black are the print inks.

qa.q: What is clear space around a logo for?
qa.right: Keeping other elements from crowding it
qa.why: It protects the logo's legibility.

qa.q: What does an Identity Programme add on top of Brand Discovery?
qa.right: Business stationery, templates, a digital asset library and editable working files
qa.why: Those items move the work from a core identity to daily-use assets.

qa.q: Which Guru Graphics pillar covers tone of voice, key messages and story?
qa.right: Brand messaging
qa.why: Messaging shapes how the brand sounds.

qa.q: What do brand guidelines set out?
qa.right: How the brand should look, sound and behave across every touchpoint
qa.why: They keep use consistent.

qa.q: Which Rollout Programme item prepares your staff to introduce the identity?
qa.right: An internal launch and staff toolkit
qa.why: The staff toolkit is internal.

qa.q: Why should you give consolidated feedback?
qa.right: It avoids contradictory instructions reaching the designer
wrong: It reduces the number of files
It removes the need for a brief
qa.why: One response beats five conflicting ones.

qa.q: What is bleed in print artwork?
qa.right: Artwork extending past the trim edge so no white edge shows
qa.why: Bleed covers small trimming shifts.

qa.q: What is a typical purpose of editable working files?
qa.right: Letting someone adapt the artwork later
wrong: Sending a logo to social media
qa.why: They contain the underlying layers and shapes.

qa.q: What does a font licence control?
qa.right: Who and what the typeface may be used for
wrong: The file format of the logo
How many words fit on a page
qa.why: Typefaces are licensed, not free to copy.

qa.q: What does a scope of design and branding only mean for a client?
qa.right: The studio does not provide software, development, hosting or support
qa.why: Those services are outside the studio's offer.

qa.q: Which approach best settles disagreements between reviewers in your organisation?
qa.right: Naming one decision-maker
qa.why: One owner avoids design by committee.

qa.q: What is Pantone mainly used for?
qa.right: Matching a named colour exactly across printers
qa.why: It is a colour matching system.

qa.q: Which standard sets widely used contrast guidance for web content?
qa.right: WCAG
qa.why: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.

qa.q: What may a stock image licence restrict?
qa.right: How and where the photograph may be used
qa.why: Licences have terms on use.

qa.q: What does a trade mark give you?
qa.right: A registered right in a name or logo
qa.why: It must be applied for and registered.

qa.q: A colleague wants to put your logo on a dark photograph and the logo is dark navy. What should they do first?
qa.right: Check for an approved logo variant made for dark backgrounds
wrong: Stretch it to fill the space
qa.why: Variants exist for this purpose.

qa.q: Three of your colleagues send the designer conflicting comments on the same concept. What should you do?
qa.right: Gather the comments into one consolidated response through your decision-maker
wrong: Forward all comments and let the designer pick
Ignore the ones you disagree with
Ask the designer to merge them without guidance
qa.why: The designer needs a single clear instruction.

qa.q: You say you dislike a concept but cannot say why. What is the most useful next step?
qa.right: Compare it with the brief and say which objective it fails
wrong: Ask for more concepts without comment
Say it needs to pop more
Ask for it in another colour at random
qa.why: Reasons let the designer revise.

qa.q: You agreed a change with the designer on the phone. What should you do afterwards?
qa.right: Confirm it in writing
wrong: Wait to see if it is done
qa.why: Written approval records the agreement.

qa.q: A printer asks for a vector logo. Which file do you send?
qa.right: An AI, EPS, SVG or vector PDF file
qa.why: Printers need scalable artwork.

qa.q: You are asked to add a new item after the scope was agreed. What is likely to follow?
qa.right: A change request that may affect time and cost
wrong: The item is added free automatically
qa.why: Changes beyond scope are handled as change requests.

qa.q: A supplier is still using a logo from before the refresh. What is the best response?
qa.right: Send them the current files from the approved library and ask them to replace the old ones
wrong: Leave it until the next print run
qa.why: Keeping old logos in use weakens consistency.

qa.q: You want to show a partner's logo on your website. What should you do?
qa.right: Get written permission first
wrong: Edit it to match your colours
qa.why: Marks belong to their owners.

qa.q: A new team member wants to install the brand font on their laptop. What should you check?
qa.right: Whether the font licence covers another user
qa.why: Licences can limit users.

qa.q: Your organisation is a public sector body writing to a buyer. How should the framing lean?
qa.right: Trust, recognition and standing apart rather than growth
qa.why: Public sector buyers respond to reputation.

qa.q: You are choosing between PNG and JPG for a logo on a slide with a coloured background. Which is better and why?
qa.right: PNG, because it supports a transparent background
wrong: JPG, because it is a vector
PNG, because it is only for print
qa.why: JPG has no transparency.

qa.q: A printed leaflet looks different in colour from your screen. What is one likely cause?
qa.right: Screens use RGB and print uses CMYK, and profiles may differ
wrong: The printer used the wrong paper size
qa.why: Colour models and profiles differ.

qa.q: You have a launch date in six weeks and need a full brand guideline set. Which is the better first step?
qa.right: Raise the date and scope early and ask for a proposal that fits
wrong: Wait until the date is closer
Assume the studio will fit it in
qa.why: Typical durations are not promises.

qa.q: You are unsure which of the four engagements suits your organisation. What can you do?
qa.right: Start a conversation about where you are and where the brand should go
qa.why: The studio helps choose the level.

qa.q: An email thread has five versions of one concept. How should you comment?
qa.right: Name the file and version you are commenting on
qa.why: Version references avoid confusion.

qa.q: You find a customer quote that reads awkwardly and want to use it on your website. What should you do?
qa.right: Publish it exactly as written or ask the author for an edit
qa.why: Altering quotes is misleading.

qa.q: You are collecting email addresses for a newsletter. What should the form say?
qa.right: What the address will be used for and how to unsubscribe, with the policy linked
wrong: That the address will be shared with anyone
qa.why: Consent has to be informed.

qa.q: A designer proposes a red-and-green status colouring in a chart. What is a concern?
qa.right: Colour alone may not be accessible to people with colour vision deficiency
wrong: Red and green are not brand colours
qa.why: Add labels or shapes.

qa.q: You need to place a logo on a very small item. Which guideline should you check?
qa.right: Minimum size
qa.why: Minimum size keeps the logo legible.

qa.q: After a launch you want to know whether the new identity is working. What does the Rollout Programme offer?
qa.right: A post-launch review and support window
qa.why: The Rollout Programme includes that review.

qa.q: Your finance team asks whether Guru Graphics can host the new website. What is the accurate answer?
qa.right: No, the studio designs brands and does not provide hosting
wrong: Yes, as part of Brand System
Yes, as part of Rollout Programme
qa.why: Hosting is outside its offer.
